entries.answer: An integral adds up quantities accumulated over an interval, and the idea is older than the notation: the area under a curve, distance travelled from speed, and total energy from power are all the same operation, because each is a total of a rate over time. The definite integral is a limit of sums over ever-finer slices, and the fundamental theorem of calculus is the result that ties it to the derivative: the integral of a rate of change is the total change, so differentiating a total gives the rate back. That connection is the reason calculus is taught as two halves of one idea rather than two techniques. The function to integrate comes from a table or, more often in practice, from solving the differential equation you had in mind, so the real work is recognising which quantity is a rate and which is a total. A definite integral carries its units from the integrand, so integrating a speed in metres per second over seconds gives metres, and forgetting that is how a textbook answer ends up in the wrong unit.

entries.answer: A derivative measures how fast something changes with respect to something else. Graphically it is the slope of the tangent line at a point. If distance is a function of time, the derivative of distance is speed; the derivative of speed is acceleration. Calculus is built on it, together with the integral, which adds up infinitely many tiny slices to get a total.
